multilevel machine|current multilevel ma: The six-level stack Level 0 Digital level, Level 1 Microarchitecture level, Level 2 Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) level, Level 3 Operating System (OS) level, Level 4 Assembly language level, Level 5 High programming language level. See [The six-level machine](#/comp4736-p1/multilevel-machines).
digital level|level 0: "Device level made of transistors and in turn transistors are made of semiconductors. AND, OR, and NOT are the building blocks of any digital circuits". See [The six-level machine](#/comp4736-p1/multilevel-machines).
AND, OR, NOT|logic gates: "the building blocks of any digital circuits". See [The six-level machine](#/comp4736-p1/multilevel-machines).
microarchitecture level|level 1|microarc: The level where the compiled machine-code instructions "are executed ... employing ALU, Registers, and Microprograms". See [The six-level machine](#/comp4736-p1/multilevel-machines).
ISA|Instruction Set Architecture|level 2: "An ISA describes the design of a Computer in terms of the basic operations it must support. The ISA is not concerned with the implementation specific details of a computer. It is only concerned with the set or collection of basic operations the computer must support.". See [The six-level machine](#/comp4736-p1/multilevel-machines).
ATmega16: "8-bit AVR microcontroller", shown as an example instruction set summary. See [The six-level machine](#/comp4736-p1/multilevel-machines).
operating system level|level 3|OS level: "Main duties : Memory management, processes execution, and system resource protection." e.g. Linux, windows, Mac. See [The six-level machine](#/comp4736-p1/multilevel-machines).
assembly language level|level 4: "Human readable language, hard to work with, time consuming, and even a simple program contains many lines.". See [The six-level machine](#/comp4736-p1/multilevel-machines).
high programming language level|level 5: "In this level people usually write programs in languages such as Java, Python, and C++.". See [The six-level machine](#/comp4736-p1/multilevel-machines).
operating system|OS: "1. A software 2. An extended machine 3. A resource manager that provides many abstraction layers". See [Software, extended machine, resource manager](#/comp4736-p1/what-the-os-is).
OS abstraction: E.g. `ssize_t read(int fd, void *buf, size_t count);` instead of the many steps of reading a hard drive directly. See [Software, extended machine, resource manager](#/comp4736-p1/what-the-os-is).
extended machine: "Operating systems turn ugly hardware into beautiful abstractions". See [Software, extended machine, resource manager](#/comp4736-p1/what-the-os-is).
resource manager: Top down view "Provide abstractions to application programs"; bottom up view "Manage pieces of complex system"; alternative view "Provide orderly, controlled allocation of resources". See [Software, extended machine, resource manager](#/comp4736-p1/what-the-os-is).
time sharing|sharing in time: One of the "two different ways" of sharing resources; CPU and Printer are time-shared. See [Software, extended machine, resource manager](#/comp4736-p1/what-the-os-is).
space sharing|sharing in space: The other way of sharing resources; RAM and Disk are space-shared. See [Software, extended machine, resource manager](#/comp4736-p1/what-the-os-is).
multiprogramming: "each program gets a fair amount of time and memory space for execution". See [Software, extended machine, resource manager](#/comp4736-p1/what-the-os-is).
kernel mode|supervisor mode: "The operating system, the most fundamental piece of software, runs in kernel mode. In this mode it has complete access to all the hardware and can execute any instruction the machine is capable of executing.". See [Kernel mode, user mode and the four x86 rings](#/comp4736-p1/kernel-and-user-mode).
user mode: "The rest of the software runs in user mode, in which only a subset of the machine instructions is available. Instructions that affect control of the machine or do Input/Output are forbidden to user-mode programs.". See [Kernel mode, user mode and the four x86 rings](#/comp4736-p1/kernel-and-user-mode).
privilege levels|security rings|rings: Intel x86 "Four privilege levels or security rings ... used for various levels of privilege and access control within the CPU, typically in an operating system context.". See [Kernel mode, user mode and the four x86 rings](#/comp4736-p1/kernel-and-user-mode).
ring 0: "(Kernel Mode): This is the most privileged level, reserved for the operating system kernel. Code running in Ring 0 has unrestricted access to all hardware and system resources. It can execute privileged instructions and manage memory, devices, and processes. Device drivers and the core operating system components run in Ring 0.". See [Kernel mode, user mode and the four x86 rings](#/comp4736-p1/kernel-and-user-mode).
ring 1|ring 2: "Operating System Services (Device Drivers, Etc.).". See [Kernel mode, user mode and the four x86 rings](#/comp4736-p1/kernel-and-user-mode).
ring 3: "(User Mode): Ring 3 is the least privileged level and is where user applications run. ... It can't execute privileged instructions directly or access hardware resources directly. Instead, it relies on system calls to request services from the operating system.". See [Kernel mode, user mode and the four x86 rings](#/comp4736-p1/kernel-and-user-mode).
system call: Named only: what Ring 3 code "relies on ... to request services from the operating system" (slide 18); the user program "issues a system call, which the kernel then translates into a procedure call to the appropriate driver". See [Controllers, drivers, busy waiting, interrupts and DMA](#/comp4736-p1/io-devices).
user interface program: The layer between the applications and the operating system, in user mode. See [Kernel mode, user mode and the four x86 rings](#/comp4736-p1/kernel-and-user-mode).
CPU: Block containing Control Unit, ALU and Registers. See [ALU, control unit, registers, fetch-decode-execute, RISC and CISC](#/comp4736-p1/cpu).
MMU: Named only, a box inside the CPU in the PC components figure. See [ALU, control unit, registers, fetch-decode-execute, RISC and CISC](#/comp4736-p1/cpu).
bus: The shared line connecting CPU, Memory and the controllers in a simple PC. See [ALU, control unit, registers, fetch-decode-execute, RISC and CISC](#/comp4736-p1/cpu).
ALU: Tanenbaum's 1-bit ALU: logical unit (AB, A + B, B̄), decoder (F₀, F₁ → enable lines) and full adder (carry in, sum, carry out); operation chosen by F₀, F₁, ENA, ENB, INVA, INC. See [ALU, control unit, registers, fetch-decode-execute, RISC and CISC](#/comp4736-p1/cpu).
F0|F1: ALU function-select inputs fed to the decoder. See [ALU, control unit, registers, fetch-decode-execute, RISC and CISC](#/comp4736-p1/cpu).
ENA|ENB: ALU enable inputs for A and B. See [ALU, control unit, registers, fetch-decode-execute, RISC and CISC](#/comp4736-p1/cpu).
INVA: ALU input that inverts A. See [ALU, control unit, registers, fetch-decode-execute, RISC and CISC](#/comp4736-p1/cpu).
INC: ALU input that adds 1 (carry in); B − A uses INVA = 1 and INC = 1. See [ALU, control unit, registers, fetch-decode-execute, RISC and CISC](#/comp4736-p1/cpu).
B − A (ALU): "B – A = B + NOT(A) + 1" with F0 F1 ENA ENB INVA INC all 1. See [ALU, control unit, registers, fetch-decode-execute, RISC and CISC](#/comp4736-p1/cpu).
control unit: The CPU part that runs the fetch-decode-execute cycle, "Microprogram OR Hardwired". See [ALU, control unit, registers, fetch-decode-execute, RISC and CISC](#/comp4736-p1/cpu).
fetch-decode-execute|instruction executi: Machine code in Memory is fetched into Registers, decoded by the Control Unit, executed by the ALU. See [ALU, control unit, registers, fetch-decode-execute, RISC and CISC](#/comp4736-p1/cpu).
compiler: Turns "High Level Code C++, Java, JavaScript" into "Machine code". See [ALU, control unit, registers, fetch-decode-execute, RISC and CISC](#/comp4736-p1/cpu).
machine code: Binary instructions placed in memory after compilation. See [The six-level machine](#/comp4736-p1/multilevel-machines).
microprogram|microprogrammed approach: Control unit implementation; the CISC approach. See [ALU, control unit, registers, fetch-decode-execute, RISC and CISC](#/comp4736-p1/cpu).
hardwired approach: Control unit implementation; the RISC approach. See [ALU, control unit, registers, fetch-decode-execute, RISC and CISC](#/comp4736-p1/cpu).
RISC: Examples AVR, ARM, MIPS; "Hardwired Approach". See [ALU, control unit, registers, fetch-decode-execute, RISC and CISC](#/comp4736-p1/cpu).
CISC: Examples AMD, Pentium, VAX; "Microprogrammed Approach". See [ALU, control unit, registers, fetch-decode-execute, RISC and CISC](#/comp4736-p1/cpu).
instruction-level parallelism|ILP: First performance improvement, "(Pipelining)". See [Pipelining: cycle time and latency, superscalar CPUs](#/comp4736-p1/pipelining).
pipelining|pipeline: Stages S1 Instruction fetch unit, S2 Instruction decode unit, S3 Operand fetch unit, S4 Instruction execution unit, S5 Write back unit working on different instructions at once. See [Pipelining: cycle time and latency, superscalar CPUs](#/comp4736-p1/pipelining).
cycle time|CT: How often one finished item leaves the line: "Every 4 hours 1 car" (one 4-hour station) vs "Every 2 hours 1 car" (stations 1, 1, 2 hours). See [Pipelining: cycle time and latency, superscalar CPUs](#/comp4736-p1/pipelining).
latency: Time for one item to go through every stage: "Latency for each car = 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 hours". See [Pipelining: cycle time and latency, superscalar CPUs](#/comp4736-p1/pipelining).
clock period|Tp: Pipelined "Tₚ = max {t₁, t₂, ⋯, tₙ}" (slide 39); no pipelining "Tₚ = t₁ + t₂ + ⋯ + tₙ". See [Pipelining: cycle time and latency, superscalar CPUs](#/comp4736-p1/pipelining).
throughput: "Throughput = 1 / Tₚ". See [Pipelining: cycle time and latency, superscalar CPUs](#/comp4736-p1/pipelining).
delay for each instruction: Pipelined "nTₚ" (slide 39); no pipelining "Tₚ". See [Pipelining: cycle time and latency, superscalar CPUs](#/comp4736-p1/pipelining).
superscalar|superscalar processor|supers: "A superscalar processor with five functional units" (ALU, ALU, LOAD, STORE, Floating point) (slide 41); two fetch/decode pipelines feeding a "Holding buffer" and execute units for Integer arithmetic, Floating-point arithmetic, Boolean operations. See [Multithreading, multicore, multiprocessors and multicomputers](#/comp4736-p1/parallel-processors).
dual pipelines: "Dual five-stage pipelines with a common instruction fetch unit". See [Multithreading, multicore, multiprocessors and multicomputers](#/comp4736-p1/parallel-processors).
holding buffer: Where decoded instructions wait for an execute unit in a superscalar CPU. See [Multithreading, multicore, multiprocessors and multicomputers](#/comp4736-p1/parallel-processors).
multithreading|hyperthreading: "Allows the CPU to hold the state of two different threads and then switch back and forth on a nanosecond time scale e.g. SPARC, the Power5, the Intel Xeon, and the Intel Core family.". See [Multithreading, multicore, multiprocessors and multicomputers](#/comp4736-p1/parallel-processors).
multicore chip|multicore|core: "CPU chips now have four, eight, or more complete processors or cores on them e.g. Intel Xeon Phi and the Tilera TilePro, more than 60 cores on a single chip.". See [Multithreading, multicore, multiprocessors and multicomputers](#/comp4736-p1/parallel-processors).
shared L2 cache: "(a) A quad-core chip with a shared L2 cache." labelled Intel. See [Multithreading, multicore, multiprocessors and multicomputers](#/comp4736-p1/parallel-processors).
separate L2 caches: "(b) A quad-core chip with separate L2 caches." labelled AMD. See [Multithreading, multicore, multiprocessors and multicomputers](#/comp4736-p1/parallel-processors).
processor-level parallelism: The heading over multiprocessors and multi-computers. See [Multithreading, multicore, multiprocessors and multicomputers](#/comp4736-p1/parallel-processors).
multiprocessor: "A single-bus multiprocessor": CPUs and one shared memory on one bus. See [Multithreading, multicore, multiprocessors and multicomputers](#/comp4736-p1/parallel-processors).
multicomputer|multi-computer: "A multicomputer with local memories": each CPU has its own local memory. See [Multithreading, multicore, multiprocessors and multicomputers](#/comp4736-p1/parallel-processors).
memory hierarchy: "A typical memory hierarchy. The numbers are very rough approximations." Registers 1 nsec <1 KB; Cache 2 nsec 4 MB; Main memory 10 nsec 1-8 GB; Magnetic disk 10 msec 1-4 TB. See [The memory hierarchy, PC, SP, PSW and EFLAGS](#/comp4736-p1/memory-and-registers).
register|registers: "Local fast memories"; "All CPUs contain some registers inside to hold key variables and temporary results". See [The memory hierarchy, PC, SP, PSW and EFLAGS](#/comp4736-p1/memory-and-registers).
PC|program counter: "contains the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched.". See [The memory hierarchy, PC, SP, PSW and EFLAGS](#/comp4736-p1/memory-and-registers).
stack pointer: "points to the top of the current stack in memory.". See [The memory hierarchy, PC, SP, PSW and EFLAGS](#/comp4736-p1/memory-and-registers).
PSW|Program Status Word: "contains the condition code bits, which are set by comparison instructions, the CPU priority, the mode (user or kernel), and various other control bits. User programs may normally read the entire PSW but typically may write only some of its fields. The PSW plays an important role in system calls and I/O.". See [The memory hierarchy, PC, SP, PSW and EFLAGS](#/comp4736-p1/memory-and-registers).
EFLAGS register: Intel x86 32-bit flags register; S = status flag, C = control flag, X = system flag; reserved bits "DO NOT USE. Always set to values previously read.". See [The memory hierarchy, PC, SP, PSW and EFLAGS](#/comp4736-p1/memory-and-registers).
CF|carry flag: "(bit 0) Set if an arithmetic operation generates a carry or a borrow out of the most-significant bit of the result; cleared otherwise. This flag indicates an overflow condition for unsigned-integer arithmetic. It is also used in multiple-precision arithmetic.". See [The memory hierarchy, PC, SP, PSW and EFLAGS](#/comp4736-p1/memory-and-registers).
PF|parity flag: "(bit 2) Set if the least-significant byte of the result contains an even number of 1 bits; cleared otherwise.". See [The memory hierarchy, PC, SP, PSW and EFLAGS](#/comp4736-p1/memory-and-registers).
AF|auxiliary carry flag: "(bit 4) Set if an arithmetic operation generates a carry or a borrow out of bit 3 of the result; cleared otherwise. This flag is used in binary-coded decimal (BCD) arithmetic.". See [The memory hierarchy, PC, SP, PSW and EFLAGS](#/comp4736-p1/memory-and-registers).
ZF|zero flag: "(bit 6) Set if the result is zero; cleared otherwise.". See [The memory hierarchy, PC, SP, PSW and EFLAGS](#/comp4736-p1/memory-and-registers).
SF|sign flag: "(bit 7) Set equal to the most-significant bit of the result, which is the sign bit of a signed integer. (0 indicates a positive value and 1 indicates a negative value.)". See [The memory hierarchy, PC, SP, PSW and EFLAGS](#/comp4736-p1/memory-and-registers).
OF|overflow flag: "(bit 11) Set if the integer result is too large a positive number or too small a negative number (excluding the sign-bit) to fit in the destination operand; cleared otherwise. This flag indicates an overflow condition for signed-integer (two's complement) arithmetic.". See [The memory hierarchy, PC, SP, PSW and EFLAGS](#/comp4736-p1/memory-and-registers).
IOPL|I/O privilege level field: "(bits 12 and 13) Indicates the I/O privilege level of the currently running program or task. The current privilege level (CPL) of the currently running program or task must be less than or equal to the I/O privilege level to access the I/O address space. The POPF and IRET instructions can modify this field only when operating at a CPL of 0.". See [The memory hierarchy, PC, SP, PSW and EFLAGS](#/comp4736-p1/memory-and-registers).
CPL|current privilege level: Named in the IOPL definition. See [The memory hierarchy, PC, SP, PSW and EFLAGS](#/comp4736-p1/memory-and-registers).
DF, IF, TF, NT, RF, VM, AC, VIF, VIP, ID: Named only in the EFLAGS figure: Direction Flag (control, bit 10), Interrupt Enable Flag (bit 9), Trap Flag (bit 8), Nested Task (bit 14), Resume Flag (bit 16), Virtual-8086 Mode (bit 17), Alignment Check (bit 18), Virtual Interrupt Flag (bit 19), Virtual Interrupt Pending (bit 20), ID Flag (bit 21). See [The memory hierarchy, PC, SP, PSW and EFLAGS](#/comp4736-p1/memory-and-registers).
cache memory|cache|L1|L2|L3: The "Practical Solution" to the "Imbalance Between CPU and Memory": "Cache memory (L1, L2, and L3)". See [Cache lines, sets, direct mapping and replacement](#/comp4736-p1/cache-mapping).
cache line|line: "Main memories and caches are divided up into fixed-size blocks (cache lines) e.g. typically 64 bytes.". See [Cache lines, sets, direct mapping and replacement](#/comp4736-p1/cache-mapping).
set (cache)|number of sets: "Number of sets = Number of cache lines/8" for an 8-way set associative cache. See [Cache lines, sets, direct mapping and replacement](#/comp4736-p1/cache-mapping).
n-way set associative: CPU-Z descriptor, e.g. "8-way set associative, 64-byte line size". See [Cache lines, sets, direct mapping and replacement](#/comp4736-p1/cache-mapping).
mapping techniques: "1. Direct mapping. 2. Associative mapping. 3. Set - Associative mapping.". See [Cache lines, sets, direct mapping and replacement](#/comp4736-p1/cache-mapping).
direct mapping: "CI = MI % (# of cache lines)"; e.g. 4 lines: CI = 3 % 4 = 3, 10 % 4 = 2, 13 % 4 = 1. See [Cache lines, sets, direct mapping and replacement](#/comp4736-p1/cache-mapping).
memory index|MI: The index of a memory block. See [Cache lines, sets, direct mapping and replacement](#/comp4736-p1/cache-mapping).
cache index|CI: The index of a cache line. See [Cache lines, sets, direct mapping and replacement](#/comp4736-p1/cache-mapping).
associative mapping|fully associative: Named only (slide 53). [unverified, from memory of Tanenbaum/standard texts] a block may go in any cache line.
set-associative mapping: Named only (slide 53). [unverified, standard definition] a block maps to one set (index % number of sets) and may go in any line of that set.
hit|miss|hit rate|miss rate: Shown in the direct-mapping trace: "Miss : 12 Hit : 3 Miss rate : 80.000% Hit rate : 20.000%". See [Cache lines, sets, direct mapping and replacement](#/comp4736-p1/cache-mapping).
caching system issues: "A. When to put a new item into the cache. B. Which cache line to put the new item in. C. Which item to remove from the cache when a slot is needed. D. Where to put a newly evicted item in the larger memory.". See [Cache lines, sets, direct mapping and replacement](#/comp4736-p1/cache-mapping).
cache replacement algorithms: "algorithms which are used to replace the existing block in the cache memory with the new fetched data". See [Cache lines, sets, direct mapping and replacement](#/comp4736-p1/cache-mapping).
LRU|Least Recently Used: Named only, replacement algorithm 1. See [Cache lines, sets, direct mapping and replacement](#/comp4736-p1/cache-mapping).
FIFO|First In First Out: Named only, replacement algorithm 2. See [Cache lines, sets, direct mapping and replacement](#/comp4736-p1/cache-mapping).
LFU|Least Frequently Used: Named only, replacement algorithm 3. See [Cache lines, sets, direct mapping and replacement](#/comp4736-p1/cache-mapping).
random (replacement): Named only, replacement algorithm 4. See [Cache lines, sets, direct mapping and replacement](#/comp4736-p1/cache-mapping).
clock algorithm: Named only, replacement algorithm 5. See [Cache lines, sets, direct mapping and replacement](#/comp4736-p1/cache-mapping).
RAM|memory: "Memory is part of computer and contains a number of cells. Programs and data are stored in memory.". See [Cache lines, sets, direct mapping and replacement](#/comp4736-p1/cache-mapping).
cell (memory): The addressable unit of memory; "Three ways of organizing a 96-bit memory": 12 × 8 bits, 8 × 12 bits, 6 × 16 bits. See [Cache lines, sets, direct mapping and replacement](#/comp4736-p1/cache-mapping).
bit: "The basic unit of memory is bit {0, 1}.". See [Cache lines, sets, direct mapping and replacement](#/comp4736-p1/cache-mapping).
byte: "1 byte = 8 bits.". See [Cache lines, sets, direct mapping and replacement](#/comp4736-p1/cache-mapping).
word: "word = 1, 2, .. Byte". See [Cache lines, sets, direct mapping and replacement](#/comp4736-p1/cache-mapping).
disk|hard disk|magnetic disk: "one or more metal platters that rotate at 5400, 7200, 10,800 RPM or more.". See [Disks and SSDs](#/comp4736-p1/disks).
platter: The rotating metal disks; figure shows 4 platters, Surface 0 to Surface 7. See [Disks and SSDs](#/comp4736-p1/disks).
read/write head: "Read/write head (1 per surface)". See [Disks and SSDs](#/comp4736-p1/disks).
arm|mechanical arm: "A mechanical arm pivots over the platters from the corner.". See [Disks and SSDs](#/comp4736-p1/disks).
cylinder: "The outer cylinders contain more sectors than the inner ones."; "Moving the arm from one cylinder to the next takes about 1 msec. Moving it to a random cylinder typically takes 5 to 10 msec". See [Disks and SSDs](#/comp4736-p1/disks).
track: The ring on a platter (slide 12); "Once the arm is on the correct track, the drive must wait for the needed sector to rotate under the head, an additional delay of 5 msec to 10 msec, depending on the drive's RPM.". See [Disks and SSDs](#/comp4736-p1/disks).
sector: The unit that must "rotate under the head"; "reading or writing occurs at a rate of 50 MB/sec on low-end disks to 160 MB/sec on faster ones.". See [Disks and SSDs](#/comp4736-p1/disks).
SSD|solid state disk: "SSDs do not have moving parts, do not contain platters in the shape of disks, and store data in (Flash) memory. they also store a lot of data which is not lost when the power is off.". See [Disks and SSDs](#/comp4736-p1/disks).
NVM Express|NVMe: Named only, the SSD's interface in the CrystalDiskInfo screenshot. See [Disks and SSDs](#/comp4736-p1/disks).
device controller|controller|adapter: "I/O units often consist of a mechanical component and an electronic component (device controller or adapter). The controller is a chip or a set of chips that physically controls the device.". See [Controllers, drivers, busy waiting, interrupts and DMA](#/comp4736-p1/io-devices).
device: The mechanical component (e.g. the hard disk). See [Controllers, drivers, busy waiting, interrupts and DMA](#/comp4736-p1/io-devices).
device driver|driver: "The software that talks to a controller, giving it commands and accepting responses, is called a device driver. the driver has to be put into the operating system so it can run in kernel mode.". See [Controllers, drivers, busy waiting, interrupts and DMA](#/comp4736-p1/io-devices).
device registers|controller registers: "Every controller has a small number of registers that are used to communicate with it." e.g. disk address, memory address, sector count, and direction (read or write). See [Controllers, drivers, busy waiting, interrupts and DMA](#/comp4736-p1/io-devices).
busy waiting|polling: "The driver then starts the I/O and sits in a tight loop continuously polling the device to see if it is done ... This method is called busy waiting and has the disadvantage of tying up the CPU polling the device until it is finished.". See [Controllers, drivers, busy waiting, interrupts and DMA](#/comp4736-p1/io-devices).
interrupt: "the driver to start the device and ask it to give an interrupt when it is finished ... When the controller detects the end of the transfer, it generates an interrupt to signal completion.". See [Controllers, drivers, busy waiting, interrupts and DMA](#/comp4736-p1/io-devices).
DMA|Direct Memory Access: "The CPU sets up the DMA chip, telling it how many bytes to transfer, the device and memory addresses involved, and the direction, and lets it go. When the DMA chip is done, it causes an interrupt.". See [Controllers, drivers, busy waiting, interrupts and DMA](#/comp4736-p1/io-devices).
interrupt controller: Box between the disk controller and the CPU in "The steps in starting an I/O device and getting an interrupt" (steps 1-4). See [Controllers, drivers, busy waiting, interrupts and DMA](#/comp4736-p1/io-devices).
interrupt handler|interrupt processing: "Interrupt processing involves taking the interrupt, running the interrupt handler, and returning to the user program" (1. Interrupt, 2. Dispatch to handler, 3. Return). See [Controllers, drivers, busy waiting, interrupts and DMA](#/comp4736-p1/io-devices).
interrupt vector: Not on the slides. [unverified, from memory of Tanenbaum] the table of interrupt-handler addresses, indexed by the device number the interrupt controller puts on the bus.
DMI|Direct Media Interface: "DMI (Direct Media Interface) bus." (slide 70); links the processor to the Platform Controller Hub. See [Buses: SCSI, USB, DMI, PCI, PCI-Express](#/comp4736-p1/buses).
Platform Controller Hub|PCH: The hub in "The structure of a large x86 system" connecting PCIe slots, SATA, USB 2.0/3.0 ports, Gigabit Ethernet. See [Buses: SCSI, USB, DMI, PCI, PCI-Express](#/comp4736-p1/buses).
SCSI|Small Computer System Interface: "a high-performance bus intended for fast disks, scanners, and other devices needing considerable bandwidth. Nowadays, we find them mostly in servers and workstations. They can run at up to 640 MB/sec.". See [Buses: SCSI, USB, DMI, PCI, PCI-Express](#/comp4736-p1/buses).
USB|Universal Serial Bus: "Any USB device can be connected to a computer and it will function immediately, without requiring a reboot.". See [Buses: SCSI, USB, DMI, PCI, PCI-Express](#/comp4736-p1/buses).
PCI|PCI bus: "An internal synchronous bus for interconnecting chips, expansion boards, and processor/memory subsystems e.g. used for connecting adapters such as hard disks, sound cards, network cards and graphics cards.". See [Buses: SCSI, USB, DMI, PCI, PCI-Express](#/comp4736-p1/buses).
PCIe|PCI-Express: "Ideal for video and graphics applications. Not using a shared bus configuration and has a devoted path, called a lane, to a single chip known as a switch.". See [Buses: SCSI, USB, DMI, PCI, PCI-Express](#/comp4736-p1/buses).
lane: "a devoted path"; "Each lane (1x) has conductors for sending and receiving data"; x1 = 1 lane, x2 = 2 lanes, x16 = 16 lanes. See [Buses: SCSI, USB, DMI, PCI, PCI-Express](#/comp4736-p1/buses).
switch (PCIe): "a single chip known as a switch" that each lane connects to. See [Buses: SCSI, USB, DMI, PCI, PCI-Express](#/comp4736-p1/buses).
shared bus: PCI/PCI-X devices and the host on one bus, contrasted with PCIe lanes to a switch. See [Buses: SCSI, USB, DMI, PCI, PCI-Express](#/comp4736-p1/buses).
SATA: Named only, a PCH connection. See [Buses: SCSI, USB, DMI, PCI, PCI-Express](#/comp4736-p1/buses).
mainframe operating systems: "(OS/390 and Linux) Room-sized computers. A mainframe with 1000 disks and millions of gigabytes of data is not unusual. They typically offer three kinds of services: batch, transaction processing, and timesharing.". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
batch|transaction processing|timesharing: "three kinds of services" mainframes offer; named only. See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
server operating systems: "(Solaris, FreeBSD, Linux and Windows Server 201x) They run on servers, which are either very large personal computers, workstations, or even mainframes.". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
multiprocessor operating systems: "(Windows and Linux)". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
personal computer operating systems: "(Linux, FreeBSD, Windows 7, Windows 8, and Apple's OS X)". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
handheld computer operating systems: "(Android and Apple's iOS)". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
embedded operating systems: "(Embedded Linux, QNX and VxWorks) Embedded systems run on the computers that control devices that are not generally thought of as computers and which do not accept user-installed software. Typical examples are microwave ovens, TV sets, cars, DVD recorders, traditional phones, and MP3 players.". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
sensor node operating systems: "(TinyOS) ... These nodes are tiny computers that communicate with each other and with a base station using wireless communication.". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
real-time operating systems: "(eCos) These systems are characterized by having time as a key parameter For example, in industrial process-control systems, real-time computers have to collect data about the production process and use it to control machines in the factory.". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
smart card operating systems: "(JVM) Some smart cards are Java oriented. This means that the ROM on the smart card holds an interpreter for the Java Virtual Machine (JVM). Java applets (small programs) are downloaded to the card and are interpreted by the JVM interpreter.". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
JVM|Java Virtual Machine: The interpreter held in a Java smart card's ROM. See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
process: "Key concept in all operating systems. program in execution. Process is associated with an address space. ... Also associated with set of resources. Process can be thought of as a container. – Holds all information needed to run program". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
address space: "Each process has some set of addresses it can use, typically running from 0 up to some maximum (address space).". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
process table: "all the information about each process, other than the contents of its own address space, is stored in an operating system table called the process table, which is an array of structures, one for each process currently in existence.". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
text segment: "the text segment (i.e., the program code)". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
data segment: "the data segment (i.e., the variables) ... The data segment grows upward". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
stack segment|stack: "and the stack segment ... the stack grows downward.". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
gap: The unused space between Data and Stack in the address-space figure. See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
base of stack: The first (highest) stack address, 100 (0x64) holding A in the figure. See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
top of stack|TOS: The most recently pushed item, 97 (0x61) holding D in the figure. See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
process tree: "Process A created two child processes, B and C. Process B created three child processes, D, E, and F.". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
child process: A process created by another process. See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
daemon: Not on the slides. [unverified, from memory of Tanenbaum] a background process that is not attached to a user, e.g. one started at boot to handle requests.
file: "Files are logical units of information created by processes."; the OS presents "a nice, clean abstract model of device-independent files". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
directory: "a way of grouping files together. File hierarchies are organized as trees." "A directory is simply a file containing a set of (i-number, ASCII name) pairs.". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
i-number: "Every file in UNIX has a unique number, its i-number, that identifies it. This i-number is an index into a table of i-nodes" (slide 80); shown by `ls -i` ("print the index number of each file"). See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
i-node|inode: One per file, "telling who owns the file, where its disk blocks are, and so on." (slide 80); figure "Inode 6": Attributes plus Disk addresses. See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
root directory: Top of the directory hierarchy. See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
path name: "Every file within the directory hierarchy can be specified by giving its path name from the root directory." e.g. /Faculty/Prof.Brown/Courses/CS101 (Unix), \Faculty\Prof.Brown\Courses\CS101 (MS_DOS). See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
file descriptor: "Before a file is read or written, it must be opened by checking the permissions. If the access is permitted, the system returns a small integer called a file descriptor to use in subsequent operations. If the access is prohibited, an error code is returned.". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
mount|mount system call: "allows the file system on the CD-ROM to be attached to the root file system wherever the program wants it to be. File systems are nearly always mounted on empty directories.". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
pipe: "a sort of pseudofile that can be used to connect two processes. One process generates some output that another process uses as input.". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
protection: "It is up to the operating system to manage the system security so that files, for example, are accessible only to authorized users.". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
protection code: "Files in UNIX are protected by assigning each one a 9-bit binary protection code. The protection code consists of three 3-bit fields, one for the owner, one for other members of the owner's group ..., and one for everyone else.". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
group: "users are divided into groups by the system administrator". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
rwx bits|protection bits: "Each field has a bit for read access, a bit for write access, and a bit for execute access. These 3 bits are known as the rwx bits." (slide 87); the nine characters after the type letter in `ls -l`. See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
- (file type)|regular file: "– : regular file". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
d (file type)|directory: "d : directory". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
c (file type)|character device file: "c : character device file". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
b (file type)|block device file: "b : block device file". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
s (file type)|local socket file: "s : local socket file". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
p (file type)|named pipe: "p : named pipe". See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
l (file type)|symbolic link: "l : symbolic link" (e.g. `l_thread -> thread.c`). See [The OS zoo, processes, files, mount, pipes and protection](#/comp4736-p1/os-zoo-processes-files).
